**Your arithmetic checks out if $180 is your machine cost and $132 is your annual courier-and-filter cost. Those figures alone do not establish that the model is sound or launch-ready.**

| Per customer | Year 1 | 36 months |
|---|---:|---:|
| Subscription revenue | $288 | $864 |
| Machine cost | −$180 | −$180 |
| Courier + filters | −$132 | −$396 |
| **Contribution before other costs** | **−$24** | **+$288** |

That assumes 36 paid months, unchanged costs, and no machine replacement. The $288 is **not net profit**: it must still cover customer acquisition, installation, servicing, payment fees, warranty claims, financing, and overhead.

At $24 revenue minus $11 recurring cost per month, you generate **$13/month toward recovering the machine cost**. On that simplified basis, payback occurs during month 14. Actual cash timing depends on when you pay for delivery and filters and collect subscriptions.

A 36-month B2B contract helps only to the extent its terms and customer credit support collection. It does not remove default, cancellation, or service obligations.

**Use this in the review:**

> “The base case produces $288 per customer over 36 months after machine, courier, and filter costs, but before acquisition, installation, service, financing, and overhead. Year-one contribution is negative $24. This supports further validation, not a full-launch decision. I recommend a capped pilot after we verify the remaining costs, contract terms, and cash requirements.”

Before 8am, put those assumptions and unknowns on one page. Read the opening rather than relying on memory after no sleep.

**My recommendation: seek approval for a costed, cash-capped pilot—not an unconditional launch.**
